article_title: This Rakhi, Celebrate Your Sister With Mia By Tanishq's New Edit | Grazia India
sub_title: Looking for Rakhi gifts for your sister? Discover five contemporary gold and diamond jewellery picks from Mia by Tanishq.
article_content: Skip the predictable and gift your sister jewellery she will wear on repeat Raksha Bandhan is a yearly reminder that some relationships deserve more than a quick 'Happy Rakhi' text and a box of chocolates. Your sister has probably spent years knowing exactly what you like, so this time, return the favour by choosing something that feels made for her. Mia by Tanishq's latest edit spans delicate florals, playful hearts, organic leaf motifs and classic paisley, all reimagined in gold and natural diamonds. From a delicate necklace that works with a crisp white shirt to diamond studs that can carry her from weekday dressing to festive plans, these five pieces are made to become part of her everyday jewellery rotation. Blossom Whisper Diamond Necklace Floral jewellery can sometimes feel overly ornate. The Blossom Whisper Diamond Necklace takes a more pared-back route, with a fine floral-inspired silhouette crafted in 9K yellow gold and set with 10 natural diamonds. The result is delicate enough for everyday wear, with just enough sparkle to catch the light. Its blooming motif makes it an especially fitting choice for Rakhi, a small nod to a bond that's kept growing since you were kids, while its understated silhouette ensures it works well beyond the occasion. Gentle Buzz Diamond Stud Earrings For the sister who likes her jewellery with a little personality, the Gentle Buzz Diamond Stud Earrings bring a playful note to the jewellery box. The heart-inspired silhouette combines 9K yellow and white gold with natural diamonds, giving the everyday stud a charming update. They are easy enough to wear on repeat, but the distinctive shape keeps them from fading into the background. Consider them a small, sparkling nod to all the affection, teasing and shared history that comes with being siblings. Playful Sparkle Leaf Diamond Bracelet The Playful Sparkle Leaf Diamond Bracelet takes its inspiration from nature, translating leaf motifs into a delicate 14K gold design embellished with natural diamonds. Its slender profile makes it an easy addition to an existing jewellery stack, whether she prefers mixing bracelets with a watch or wearing a single piece at a time. The organic detailing gives it a playful edge without making it feel too precious. For the sister who likes her accessories to have a little movement and character, this one should fit right in. Radiant Arc Diamond Stud Earrings Inspired by the movement of sun rays, the Radiant Arc Diamond Stud Earrings bring a more graphic touch to the edit. Crafted in 14K yellow gold and set with 16 natural diamonds, the radiating design catches the light as it moves. Their versatility is a major part of the appeal. Wear them with workwear during the week, then pair them with an evening look when the occasion calls for a little more sparkle. For a sister stepping into a new chapter, they also carry the optimistic symbolism of light and forward movement. Lucid Lens Evil Eye Gold Necklace The evil eye has been worn as protection for centuries, rooted in the same basic instinct to guard against whatever bad luck might be circling. The Lucid Lens Evil Eye Gold Necklace puts that symbolism at the centre of the design, with a mesmerising blue synthetic stone set within a 14K yellow gold eye motif. The deep blue stone provides the necklace its focal point, while the gold setting brings definition to its delicate silhouette. It works whether she actually believes in this or likes what it stands for. Either way, gift it because you'd rather she had a little extra luck on her side than not. Mia by Tanishq's edit covers plenty of jewellery personalities, from floral and nature-inspired designs to playful hearts and enduring paisley. This Rakhi, pick the piece that feels most like her, and give her a reason to reach for it long after the rakhi has been tied. article_title: Abu Jani Sandeep Khosla Just Turned Maximalism Into a 20,000-Sq-Ft Fantasy | Grazia India
sub_title: Step inside Mubarak Baug, Abu Jani Sandeep Khosla’s extravagant new Mumbai flagship celebrating 40 years of maximalist Indian design.
article_content: Inside Abu Jani Sandeep Khosla’s 40th year: A Mumbai flagship built to defy reality. You walk into the iconic Framjee Cawasjee Institute in South Mumbai expecting a certain amount of drama. This is Abu Jani Sandeep Khosla, after all. You know the vocabulary: Mirror work, chikankari , zardozi , bridal grandeur, unapologetic colour and maximalism dialled all the way up. And yet, when you first enter Mubarak Baug, it feels almost… normal . Polished, considered – a rather elegant store. Then you walk upstairs. And suddenly, everything is gold. The walls glow, chandeliers hang overhead like enormous pieces of jewellery, gilded bamboo racks frame couture, and golden screens create little corridors within corridors. Mirrors reflect mirrors, multiplying the light. Above you, mythical swans appear to be flying through the ceiling, while an entire city – handcrafted in brass – hangs upside down overhead. You stop and stare – because it feels more like Charlie and the Chocolate Factory if Willy Wonka had replaced every drop of chocolate with molten gold. Tell Sandeep Khosla exactly that and he laughs. It is, as it turns out, not far from the brief. Mubarak Baug, which translates to ‘a garden of celebration’, is the 20,000-square-foot fantasy world Abu Jani Sandeep Khosla has created to mark the beginning of its 40th year. Designed by A Wonder Room, the house’s interior design vertical, it is part flagship, part archive, part museum, part art gallery and entirely AJSK. “We get India in its maximal form here,” Khosla shares. “Because Abu and I are, first, maximalists. And we are unapologetic about our maximalism. We own it, we love it” he adds. At Mubarak Baug, maximalism is a worldview. Nothing exists in isolation. Couture sits beside art, craft becomes architecture, flowers become installations, food becomes part of the experience. Even the smallest details refuse to behave modestly. Look at the floral arrangements and you’ll notice red glass bangles woven into them – an ode to brides, because AJSK is, at its heart, a house deeply intertwined with Indian bridal culture. Look at the table and you’ll find an indulgent feast, including a particularly delicious minced lamb loaf with apricots and prunes. It has nothing to do with fashion, technically, but somehow everything to do with the AJSK universe. Because why should the food be restrained when the interiors certainly aren’t? “Nobody eats one dish for lunch or dinner. So all of you are maximalists. Do not deny that” – says Khosla. You would be hard-pressed to argue with him while standing beneath a chandelier the size of a small apartment. But the real surprise comes when you reach the uppermost floor because the archives are at the top. Here, the house’s four-decade history is presented not as a conventional retrospective, but as a treasure vault. You come face-to-face with pieces that have entered the mythology of Indian fashion: The Architectural AJSK Coat, exquisite chikankari , lavish vasli and the real mirror ghagra worn by Madhuri Dixit in Devdas (2002). The ghagra catches the light as you move around it, each mirror revealing another tiny reflection. It is the actual garment from the film for which Abu Jani Sandeep Khosla received the National Award for Best Costume Design in 2003. Seeing it outside the context of a film set makes the craftsmanship feel even more extraordinary. What once moved across a screen now sits still, allowing you to appreciate the thousands of hours hidden inside its surface. “Our chikankari , mirror work, zardozi collections are our hallmark collections. They best represent the finesse and standard of our work which is continuously evolving”, Khosla says. You see that evolution in the older cholis and dupattas displayed alongside later masterpieces – pieces reminiscent of the early days when Abu Jani and his mother worked on intricate embroideries themselves. The juxtaposition makes the passage of time tangible: The same obsession with handwork, reimagined across four decades. It is one thing to read that Abu and Sandeep have spent their careers reviving Indian craft. It is another to stand inches away from the evidence. And everywhere you turn, the same philosophy has been translated into architecture. The entrance corridor is an art gallery featuring the work of Shine Shivan, whose surreal, mythological imagery unfolds across the walls. Hundreds of miniature jharokas decorate the interiors. Gilded screens carve the space into intimate passages. Embroidered remnants from the atelier have been repurposed into decorative installations, giving discarded materials another life. Above the ready-to-wear section, an enormous ‘Inverted City’ hangs from the ceiling in brass, while crystal chandeliers glitter beside it. The black granite floor beneath feels almost like a night sky. And then you look up to see huge, mythical, hand-carved swans flying among illuminated clouds. That sense of fantasy is rooted in something far more serious: A fierce belief in Indian design. “India is so fantastically born. And so fantastic to create. But the tragedy is we all look down on India,” Khosla says. “We are so busy promoting various cultures that we have forgotten our own culture,” he adds. Here, India is not softened, edited or translated. It is amplified. You see it in the embroidery, the architecture, the materials, the hospitality and the sheer density of detail. It is craft in its most extravagant form. “India is our Eternal Muse.Our clothes are distinctly and unabashedly Indian” Khosla explains. The building itself becomes part of that story. The Framjee Cawasjee Institute dates back to Bombay’s earlier life, and its metropolitan, Art Deco spirit has been woven into the interiors. An embossed Bombay skyline forms one of the store’s most striking corridors, while elements of the design trace back to an old sketch created by Abu Jani. “It’s Abu and me in a way. It’s yin and yang, there’s duality,” Khosla explains. “And it also kind of formed out of a sketch, a very old sketch that Abu made many, many years ago.” The duality is everywhere. Bombay and Mumbai. Archive and future. Couture and architecture. Tradition and reinvention. Abu and Sandeep. The partnership began on 15 August 1986, when the two met at a mutual friend’s home as complete strangers. By the end of the day, they had decided to work together. They had little money but they had an instinct. Their parents gave them ₹50,000 each, and they spent it on fabric. And they never looked back. Now, at 40, comes Mubarak Baug. “The vision for Mubarak Baug was to create a fantasy world that embodies the essence of Abu Jani Sandeep Khosla,” Khosla says. “It is 40 years of AJSK contained in one palatial space, in which the past is honoured, and the present is cherished with an excitement for the future.” And you can feel that tension between past and future everywhere. At Mubarak Baug, you don’t have to be persuaded. You walk through the gilded corridors. You look at the couture. You notice the bangles in the flowers. You stare at Madhuri Dixit’s mirror ghagra. You look up at the swans. You get lost in the reflections. And eventually, you understand that for Abu Jani Sandeep Khosla, maximalism isn’t about having too much – it is about refusing to have too little. After four decades, Mubarak Baug is their most extravagant proof yet. An ode to India, to craft, to Bombay, to friendship – and to the glorious, slightly mad idea that if you can dream it, you might as well gild it. article_title: How Tribe Amrapali Brought Ramayana's Jewellery to Life | Grazia India
sub_title: Explore how Tribe Amrapali created nearly 4000 handcrafted jewellery pieces that shape the visual identity of Ramayana through craft storytelling and design.
article_content: A deep dive into the gold, gemstones, and craftsmanship shaping the visual world of Ramayana. In the world of the Ramayana , jewellery is not subtle. It gleams, stacks, cascades, frames the face and, in Ravana's case, almost armours the body. But for all its visual grandeur, the jewellery created for Nitesh Tiwari's much-anticipated epic does more than simply make its characters look the part. It is giving each of them a distinct fashion language. Nearly 4,000 handcrafted pieces went into building this world, and the number only means something once you've seen what it was spent on. This wasn't a costume department working through a checklist. It was closer to character development, carried out in gold and silver. We already know this story. Most audiences walking into the theatre will know how it ends. But look closely at what everyone is wearing, and there's still something new to read. The Armour of Lanka Ravana's jewellery operates on a logic of pure intimidation. His gold-plated collar sits high across the collarbones like a piece of ceremonial plate armour, hammered in deep repoussé, heavy with floral scrollwork, and anchored by midnight-blue cabochon stones. Gemstone-studded forearm cuffs and a kamarbandh of layered crimson and blue medallions push the silhouette outward until it takes up more room than the man wearing it needs, sculpted upper-arm cuffs adding another layer of weight before you even reach the rings on his hands.  Ravana wears his jewellery like a second skin of armour. His opulent adornments become wearable battlements, blurring the line between luxury and power. Decoding Lord Rama’s Aesthetic Where Ravana demands space, Lord Ram occupies it through balance instead. His look avoids drama in favour of geometry, with layered gold chains tapering towards a single medallion, sculpted keyuras hugging the biceps, and broad engraved wrist cuffs that read more like discipline than decoration. A repoussé-worked mekhala grounds the whole thing at the waist, its embossed motifs catching light without ever pulling focus away from the man wearing it. Set against Lanka's aggression, Lord Ram's jewellery reflects that restraint, held with enough conviction, can be its own kind of power. The Artistry Behind Maa Sita Maa Sita's jewellery works through accumulation rather than volume. Chokers nestle beneath longer, fluid chains, a slender nath traces the jawline, jhumkas and a fine maang tikka catch the light close to the face. Soft hair adornments finish the look at the crown, reflecting her divine femininity. At the wrists, thin bangles stack in dense filigree rather than standing apart as individual statement pieces, and slim rings pick up the same floral detailing running through the rest of the set. The details of the whole look feel rich without feeling heavy, which is a harder thing to design than it looks on screen. Heirlooms of Ayodhya, Anchoring King Dashrath King Dashrath's jewellery carries itself like a man who has held his throne long enough not to need reminding. Graduated gold chains fall across the chest in careful layers, anchored by a substantial repoussé pendant carved with motifs that feel handed down rather than freshly cast for a scene. Heavy armlets, stacked cuffs, an ornate belt and a signet ring finish the look, each piece doing its job without competing for attention, embodying the wisdom, dignity and enduring legacy of Ayodhya's revered monarch. The Exile Where The Gold Comes Off The fourteen-year exile marks the sharpest turn in the entire collection. The gold and gemstones disappear, and what's left is raw and tactile: Rudraksha malas layered at the neck, natural cord replacing chain, simple beaded armlets shared across Lord Ram, Maa Sita and Laxman. Maa Sita's version keeps only the barest accents, a petite nose pin, a pair of small drop earrings, slender bangles that do not attempt ornament, everything else stripped back to almost nothing. It's the strongest storytelling decision in the whole collection. The characters have changed settings, their circumstances have changed, and the jewellery tracks that shift as precisely as any costume change could. Shedding the ornamentation is a design shift that makes absence feel far more deliberate than royal excess. The Craft Behind the Characters None of this happened by instinct alone. Tarang Arora, Creative Head at House of Amrapali, has been clear that the brief was never to build costumes. "It was about building the visual grammar of the Ramayana universe through ornamentation," he said, describing a process where every character needed a distinct design philosophy while still belonging to one cohesive world, Ayodhya's restraint and Lanka's excess feeling as they came from the same universe without ever reading as the same style. Getting there took months of historical, cartographic and cultural research, tracing the sacred geographies and metallurgical traditions folded into the epic long before a single piece was fabricated. "Every motif, texture, silhouette and handcrafted detail carries narrative intent," Arora added, and across nearly 4,000 pieces, that intent holds. Techniques like repoussé, granulation, filigree, and hand chasing all belong to craft traditions centuries older than the film itself, brought back into use not as decoration but as a way of making the fantasy feel real. The full scale of the work will be clearer once the film is out. For now, the trailer alone makes a strong case that the jewellery isn't an afterthought in this production and is doing some of the heaviest visual storytelling. article_title: Behind PT Usha's Commonwealth Games 2026 Ceremonial Looks By Shantnu Nikhil | Grazia India
sub_title: In conversation with Shantnu Nikhil about dressing PT Usha for Commonwealth Games 2026 Closing Ceremony in Glasgow
article_content: The designer duo on dressing the athlete as she represented the country at CG 2026 We unpack the three bespoke looks worn by PT Usha at the Commonwealth Games 2026 ceremonies by Shantnu Nikhil. The Opening Ceremony look symbolises a sense of ceremony and resilience through rich tonal brocades and velvet detailing and then moves on to the elongated silhouette and cascading metallic leaf embroidery for the official engagement look and the emerald brocade ensemble, where India's identity becomes central to the narrative for the Closing Ceremony. GRAZIA: What was the thought behind PT Usha's look at the Commonwealth Games flag during the Closing Ceremony in Glasgow? Shantnu Nikhil: The world knows PT Usha through photographs that have become part of India's collective memory. On the track, in motion, in victory. At Shantnu Nikhil, our instinct was to turn the lens around. We wanted to understand the woman behind those images. Through our conversations and personal fittings, we weren't simply designing for the Commonwealth Games; we were getting to know someone whose humility, grace and strength have remained unchanged despite a lifetime of extraordinary achievement. That became the foundation of the three bespoke looks we created for her Commonwealth Games journey in Glasgow. For the Closing Ceremony, where she received the Commonwealth Games flag on behalf of India, choosing an Indian-woven emerald brocade felt like the most authentic place to begin, reflecting the country she has represented with unwavering pride throughout her life. The elongated silhouette speaks to authority, while the cascading leaf embroidery with cherry accents became the emotional anchor of the design. As we spent time with PT Usha, we kept returning to the idea that her legacy was never defined by a single victory, but by decades of resilience, perseverance and continual growth. The leaf became our interpretation of that journey, symbolising endurance, evolution and the many milestones that together shape a legacy. In many ways, the ensemble became a portrait of PT Usha herself: Understated, resilient and powerful. It embodies the Maison's vision of contemporary Indian ceremonial dressing while honouring a woman who continues to inspire generations. G: What did dressing PT Usha for this occasion mean for you both? SN: Designing for PT Usha became far more personal than we had imagined. As the conversations unfolded and the fittings became more frequent, we found ourselves talking less about clothes and more about her journey, what this moment meant to her, and how she wanted to feel representing India once again. That's when the process shifted. We weren't simply creating three bespoke looks anymore. We were shaping a visual narrative around a woman who has spent a lifetime representing the country with extraordinary grace. Every decision that followed became instinctive. G: How was PT Usha's personal sense of style integrated in this outfit? SN: From our very first fitting, it became clear that ease was as important as elegance. That informed every decision we made. The silhouettes were elongated and refined, the embellishment remained purposeful, and every detail was carefully edited to ensure nothing distracted from the person wearing it. The result wasn't about changing her style. It was about elevating what already exists so naturally within her. G: How did you translate the significance of the Commonwealth Games flag handover into the design? SN: As the Commonwealth Games make their way to India for the centenary edition in 2030, it marks the beginning of a new chapter and the responsibility of carrying forward the spirit and legacy of the Games. We wanted the designs to reflect that sense of optimism, pride and purpose. Rather than treating each occasion in isolation, we approached the three bespoke looks as one considered journey. Each silhouette was designed to respond to a different moment, gradually building towards the Closing Ceremony, where she accepted the Commonwealth Games flag on behalf of India. There is a progression across the three looks. The Opening Ceremony introduces a sense of ceremony and resilience through rich tonal brocades and velvet detailing. The official engagement look expresses confidence through its elongated silhouette and cascading metallic leaf embroidery. By the Closing Ceremony, that language reaches its fullest expression in the emerald brocade ensemble, where India's identity becomes central to the narrative. For us, it was never about creating three separate looks. It was about creating three chapters of the same story, one that honours where the Games have been, celebrates where India stands today, and looks ahead to where they are going next. G: Were there any specific references – Indian heritage, sport, architecture or contemporary culture that influenced your design process? SN: The strongest reference was PT Usha herself. Once we spent time with her, we realised her life already embodies everything we wanted to express. Each of the three bespoke looks was created for a distinct moment in her Commonwealth Games journey, but together they form one narrative. We wanted every element to carry meaning. Choosing Indian-woven brocades felt instinctive, a reflection of the country she has so proudly represented throughout her life. The elongated silhouettes express authority, while the recurring cascading leaf motif became the defining thread across all three looks. Traditionally associated with growth and renewal, we reinterpreted it as an ode to triumph, perseverance and the many victories that shape not just an individual, but a nation. Its movement across each silhouette reflects a legacy that has continued to evolve over decades, never standing still, always moving forward. That balance between symbolism and restraint has always been central to the way we design. The references are unmistakably Indian, yet expressed through a contemporary language that reflects the Maison's enduring dialogue between heritage and contemporary form. G: International sporting events have now become platforms for cultural storytelling through fashion. How do you see this moment contributing to India's global image? SN: Fashion has always been an integral part of a nation's cultural storytelling. It carries identity, pride and a sense of belonging long before a word is spoken. As a Maison, we've always been deeply connected to the world of sport. Whether it's cricket, golf or tennis, we've experienced first-hand how sport shapes character, discipline and ambition. Those values have naturally found their way into the way we design. Dressing PT Usha for the Commonwealth Games felt like a natural extension of that philosophy. It wasn't about creating bespoke looks for an international stage; it was about celebrating a woman who has shaped India's sporting identity for generations. We believe moments like these present a different image of India to the world, one that is confident in its heritage, contemporary in its expression and unafraid to let fashion become part of its cultural narrative. G: How long did the design process take and what were some of the biggest creative challenges? SN: The process unfolded over several weeks, with every fitting helping us understand PT Usha a little better. The biggest challenge wasn't arriving at the final designs, it was knowing when they felt complete. Every detail, whether it was the proportion of a silhouette or the placement of an embroidered motif, had to earn its place. When you're designing for someone whose story already carries so much meaning, the instinct isn't to add more. It's to edit with intention. That sense of restraint became one of the defining principles of the entire process. Disclaimer: This article offers general fashion and lifestyle inspiration. article_title: The Chicest Ways To Style Capri Pants And Cropped Trousers | Grazia India
sub_title: From Monaco-inspired minimalism to statement tailoring, discover seven fresh ways to style capri pants and cropped trousers this season.
article_content: The once-controversial hemline gets a thoroughly modern makeover. Once relegated to the fashion archives alongside butterfly clips and low-rise denim, capri pants are making their most unexpected comeback yet. The mid-calf silhouette spent years caught between nostalgic Y2K styling and practical vacation wear, but as designers revisit late ’90s minimalism, sharper tailoring, and more experimental proportions, cropped trousers have officially reclaimed their place in the fashion conversation. The secret to making them feel modern? It’s all in the styling. Today’s It girls are swapping predictable pairings for polished contrasts, balancing the shortened silhouette with oversized tailoring, statement textures, and elevated accessories. From Monaco-inspired minimalism to after-dark glamour, here’s how to make fashion’s most controversial hemline feel intentional, sophisticated, and undeniably chic. Clean-Girl Riviera Take a pair of sleek, knee-grazing black capris, preferably with subtle lace side slits for movement, and pair them with a clean ribbed white cami. The result is high-octane European summer meets effortless ’90s minimalism. Style Tip: High-shine leather thong heels and narrow oval sunglasses instantly elevate the look from beachside basics to paddock-side glamour. Keep jewellery understated with a single cuff or minimalist studs. A post shared by Tania Shroff (@tania_shroff) Faux Fur Fixes Everything Denim capris get a dramatic upgrade when styled alongside a statement fur or faux fur coat and a barely-there crop top. Let the outerwear create the impact while the denim keeps the silhouette grounded. It’s plush volume up top paired with sleek precision below. Style Tip: Add heeled sandals and a bold pop of colour through a bag, cap, or accessory to keep the contrast between casual denim and evening glamour feeling fresh. A post shared by rock revival (@rockrevival) French Girl Park Chic Swap your usual denim shorts for light-wash pedal pushers. Layer an unbuttoned white linen shirt, casually tied at the waist, over a fitted tank top for a look that feels sun-drenched, relaxed, and effortlessly put together. Style Tip: Lean into the vintage mood with a printed silk scarf, classic ballet flats, and a timeless shoulder bag. A post shared by Khushi Kapoor (@khushikapoor) Quiet Luxury Off-Duty Master effortless proportions by playing with opposing silhouettes. Contrast narrow, structured cropped pants with an oversized, relaxed button-down left unbuttoned up top. The casual volume on top balances the abbreviated hem below for a refined, model-off-duty feel. Style Tip: Complete the look with clear or kitten-heeled mules and a structured carry-all tote bag to ground the fluid tailoring. A post shared by Barbara Palvin (@realbarbarapalvin) The Downtown Cool Girl For those ready to embrace the early 2000s revival fully, lean into utility-inspired silhouettes. Think low-rise camo capris, distressed details, lace accents, and a playful micro top for a look that channels pop-star rebellion with a contemporary twist. Style Tip : Balance the heavier, military-inspired bottoms with delicate footwear like colourful ballet flats. Finish with oversized hoops, layered chains, or a statement belt. A post shared by Up Next (@upnextdesigner) The Jet-Setter Power Suit Cropped trousers aren’t just for casual dressing. A structured co-ord set featuring a fitted buttoned jacket and tailored slit-hem trousers proves that shorter hemlines can hold their own in professional and travel wardrobes. Style Tip: Classic pointed pumps visually elongate the leg, while oversized sunglasses add a celebrity-approved finishing touch. A post shared by Runway x Red Carpet | Fashion (@runwayxredcarpet) The New Occasion Wear For a couture-inspired take, look beyond traditional eveningwear and embrace embroidered cropped tailoring. An intricately detailed brocade capri suit layered over a sheer black turtleneck brings together traditional craftsmanship and modern silhouettes. The result? A look that feels regal, dramatic, and completely fashion-forward. Style Tip: Match your heels to the metallic threadwork, pull your hair into a sleek bun, and let the embroidery take centre stage. A post shared by Sanya Kapoor (@sanyakapoor) Forget the old rules about where a hemline should land. Styled with strict lines, unexpected volume, and sharp footwear, the cropped trouser is no longer a challenging piece but the most versatile piece in your rotation. article_title: Everything On Our Style Radar This Month | Grazia India
sub_title: Burberry reimagines its signature House Check, while Verlas brings lab-grown diamonds and New Balance adds their latest runner shoes to your everyday wardrobe.
article_content: The most exciting launches in fashion this month OLD MONEY, NEW BAG Burberry’s refreshed House Check collection makes heritage feel effortlessly modern F ew motifs are as instantly recognisable – or as intensely woven into fashion history – as the beige, black and red tartan that has come to define Burberry. It’s back this season, on a refreshed lineup of bags that prove classics are classics for a reason. The British House has unveiled a new collection of House Check canvas bags, reimagining some of its best-loved silhouettes while introducing a handful of fresh additions. Drawing from archival shapes and motifs, the collection celebrates the brand’s heritage without feeling nostalgic for nostalgia’s sake. Leading the revival is the return of the ‘Pocket’ bag, alongside familiar favourites including bucket bags and spacious holdalls. Joining them are two new silhouettes: The travel-ready ‘Zip Tote’ and the softly curved ‘Primrose’ bag, both finished with detachable gold-plated Knight charms that nod to Burberry’s historic Equestrian Knight emblem. Across the collection, the signature archive beige House Check is paired with smooth leather trims and refined hardware, striking the balance between practicality and polish. As fashion continues to embrace investment dressing over impulse buys, heritage bags are enjoying a renaissance. Consumers are gravitating towards pieces with a story – bags that transcend seasonal trends and carry decades of design history with them. Whether slung over a trench coat or paired with lived-in denim, the refreshed collection reminds us why the House Check has endured for over a century. A NEW ERA OF DIAMONDS Verlas brings lab – grown diamonds into your everyday wardrobe rotation G one are the days when diamonds lived in safes. Verlas reimagines them as everyday essentials, crafting IGI-certified lab-grown diamonds in BIS hallmarked 9K and 14K gold across yellow, white and rose gold. From the floral romance of ‘La Fleur’ to the geometric edge of ‘Zenyth’ and the stack-friendly versatility of ‘Octad’, each collection is designed to fit seamlessly into your daily wardrobe. Its everyday necklace and ring collections champion timeless pieces that are equally suited to layering, gifting or wearing solo. Modern, wearable and thoughtfully designed, Verlas proves that fine jewellery isn’t reserved for milestones – it belongs in your everyday rotation. Explore the collections at Verlas.in. YOUR NEXT SOLE MATE Meet the AC Runner – the all-rounder designed for sprints, squats and everything in between R unning shoes are no longer reserved solely for the track. With hybrid workouts, strength training and recovery sessions all packed into the same week, versatility has become the new performance metric – and New Balance’s latest launch is designed with exactly that in mind. Enter the AC Runner, the brand’s newest performance trainer that seamlessly transitions from conditioning runs and gym sessions to team sports and everyday wear. At its core is New Balance’s signature Fresh Foam X midsole, delivering plush cushioning for long-lasting comfort, while three levels of foam firmness provide the responsiveness needed for everything from explosive lateral drills to steady cardio sessions. The lightweight mesh upper keeps things breathable, while contemporary printed graphics ensure the AC Runner looks just as good paired with your off-duty athleisure as it does on the training floor. Enhanced lateral and linear stability round out the design, making it a dependable choice for anyone whose workouts rarely fit into a single box. article_title: Dopamine Dressing Is Bringing Bold Colour Back This Summer | Grazia India
sub_title: Dopamine dressing is this summer's biggest styling mood. Discover the psychology behind the trend and bold colour-blocking combinations to try now.
article_content: This season celebrates bold colour-blocking, joyful dressing and unexpected pairings. If fashion had a mood board this season, it wouldn't be filled with muted linens or whisper-soft tailoring. Instead, it'd be awash with butter yellow, cherry red, cobalt blue and pistachio green, colours that don't just sit next to each other but play off one another. After seasons of restraint, maximalism is making its presence felt again. And while that doesn't necessarily mean sequins at brunch or head-to-toe prints, it does mean one thing: colour is back in the spotlight. Enter dopamine dressing, a styling philosophy that embraces vibrant hues and unexpected colour pairings, proving that getting dressed can be just as much about how an outfit feels as how it looks. Despite what the name suggests, dopamine dressing isn't rooted in neuroscience as much as it is in emotion. There's no evidence that slipping into a bright orange co-ord suddenly boosts your dopamine levels, but psychologists have long acknowledged the relationship between clothing, confidence and self-perception. What we wear can influence our mood, and colour has always been one of fashion's most expressive tools. Let me hold your hand when I say this: We've romanticised beige for long enough. Somewhere between the rise of quiet luxury and the capsule wardrobe, we collectively decided that looking expensive meant looking colourless. Fashion has a short memory, though, and this season the mood has shifted. Colour is once again turning even the simplest outfit into something worth a second look. Colour-blocking, done well, isn't about wearing every bright shade you own at once. It's choosing two colours that create tension in the best possible way, letting them carry the outfit while everything else, shoes, bag, jewellery, stays quiet enough to let them. Butter Yellow + Cherry Red The unofficial colour pairing of the season. Butter yellow has all the softness of a neutral, while cherry red injects just enough contrast to keep it interesting. Together, they feel polished, playful and reminiscent of a European summer mood board. A post shared by LOEWE (@loewe) Cobalt Blue + Tangerine Orange Equal parts Mediterranean postcard and fashion-week street style, cobalt and tangerine bring out the best in each other. One cool, one warm, the balance makes the pairing feel energetic rather than overwhelming. Tomato Red + Bubblegum Pink Forget everything you were once told about these two clashing. The pairing has become a runway favourite precisely because it feels confident without trying too hard. Wear it with clean tailoring or breezy separates and let the colours do the talking. Hot Pink + Lime Green Not for the faint-hearted, but that's rather the point. This combination leans into fashion's playful side without tipping into costume territory; think oversized shirts, slip dresses, or coordinated separates. Lilac + Pistachio Green A softer entry point for anyone easing into colour-blocking. Fresh, airy and quietly elegant, it's proof that bold styling doesn't always require high-contrast shades to make an impact. Emerald Green + Electric Blue Jewel tones are having a moment, and this is one of the easiest ways to wear them. Rich, saturated and effortlessly glamorous, it works just as well for evening as it does during the day. Lavender + Bright Orange An unlikely duo that somehow feels completely natural. Lavender tempers orange's vibrancy, while orange keeps lavender from tipping into overly delicate territory. Playful, modern, and guaranteed to stand out. article_title: How Birthstones Are Turning Into Personal Markers Of Intention | Grazia India
sub_title: Birthstone jewellery is becoming a meaningful expression of astrology, numerology and deeply personal intention.
article_content: Charts, numbers and intention are redefining personal jewellery Astrology and numerology are not suddenly everywhere; culture, language and design, they are now shaping how jewellery is chosen, worn and understood. Birthstones, once symbolic, are becoming deeply personal markers of intention. Before astrology becomes belief, it begins as curiosity. Before numerology is understood, it is felt – a sense that some things align, while others resist. Jewellery is giving form to this intuition, transforming birthstones into something wearable, deliberate and quietly resonant. To understand numerology’s role in jewellery, Mumbai-based Numero Vastu consultant Biindu Khuraana begins not with belief, but with lineage. “The science of gemstones, which is called gemology, is an ancient science coming to us from the Rigveda ,” she explains. In this framework, gemstones are not ornamental afterthoughts but precise energetic tools. Each number corresponds to a planet, a gemstone, a metal, a colour, and even the specific finger on which a piece should be worn. The body, in this system, becomes part of the equation. “These gemstones are often considered as triggering the nerve of the finger they are worn on, giving benefits for the purpose they are chosen for,” she adds. Numerology, in this sense, is exacting. There are foundational rules governing how a gemstone should be worn to be effective. It must touch the skin. It should be energised through ritualistic mantras. Timing matters: The correct day, date and hour are crucial. Metal is not interchangeable, and even the hand on which a piece is worn carries significance. Traditionally, men wear gemstones on the right hand and women on the left, although working women are often advised to wear them on the right as well. From there, the system becomes highly individualised. “Those born on dates that reduce to the number one, such as the first, 10th, 19th or 28th, are advised to wear a ruby set in gold, worn on the ring finger at sunrise on a Sunday. Number two births align with pearls in silver, worn on the little finger at moonrise on a Monday. Each number unfolds its own logic: Emeralds for number five, diamonds for number six, cat’s eye for number seven, blue sapphire for number eight, and coral for number nine – each with its prescribed finger, metal and timing,” says Khuraana. The intention behind these choices is as important as the stone itself. “The benefits of gemstones are plenty,” Khuraana notes. Confidence, clarity, relationships, finances and intuition – each stone supports a different dimension of life. Design, too, plays a role. A ruby shaped like the sun can support career growth; a pearl designed as a moon may enhance emotional peace; a triangular setting can amplify Jupiter’s expansive energy. In today’s world, she adds, science and spirituality no longer exist in opposition. Worn as rings, pendants, bracelets or discreet trinkets, gemstones can be both meaningful and aesthetic – proof that alignment, too, can be beautiful. While birthstones are commonly assigned by month, astrology, as Hindu pandit Mohit Setpal explains, operates on a far more intricate level. “Birthstones are a general concept,” he says – useful, but ultimately broad. They are typically linked to a single planetary influence associated with the month of birth. For true astrological alignment, however, this is only the beginning. Setpal, who has carried forward the astrological legacy of his grandfather and has been practising for over 12 years, explains that an individual cannot be understood through one planetary placement alone. “For an individual, a total of 16 charts have to be studied,” he says. In Vedic astrology, the moment of birth is interpreted through these 16 charts, each mapping a specific area of life and its planetary alignments. “The first chart is the lagna ,” Setpal explains, “which gives a basic understanding of a person’s identity.” It forms the foundation: How an individual presents themselves to the world, their temperament and their natural inclinations. From there, the system becomes increasingly specific. “The saptamansh chart offers insight into children and lineage, while the navmansh chart focuses on marriage and the relationship with one’s spouse. Each chart highlights different planetary strengths and vulnerabilities, revealing where support may be needed, and where excess could be disruptive,” he says. This layered approach is what makes gemstone selection so precise. A stone traditionally considered beneficial may not be universally so. “On the basis of reading each of these charts,” Setpal explains, “one can suggest wearing or avoiding certain birthstones.” The aim is not to amplify every planetary influence, but to correct imbalance – strengthening weakened energies while restraining those that may already dominate. In this context, jewellery becomes a form of fine-tuning rather than symbolism. Two individuals born under the same sign may wear entirely different stones depending on how planets behave across their charts. A gemstone that supports one person’s relationships could unsettle another’s career; one that enhances clarity for one wearer might overwhelm another emotionally. Astrology, as Setpal frames it, is less about prescription and more about precision. Birthstones are not rejected but refined – filtered through the deeper intelligence of the chart. When worn correctly, jewellery moves beyond tradition and trend, becoming a personal intervention designed to support the life an individual is actually living. In an era where jewellery trends change by the season, the question arises: How do we balance fashion with pieces aligned to who we truly are? Setpal’s answer is as meticulous as it is revealing. “As I mentioned, a total of 16 charts must be studied – the lagna , saptamansh , navmansh – and one must also consider the current dasha, or planetary period,” he says. “Only then can a conclusion be drawn about which gemstone or piece of jewellery will bring balance to an individual’s life.” It is a subtle calibration. The goal is not to reject fashion, but to weave it with intention – ensuring that what adorns the wearer supports their energy, their timing and their life’s trajectory. In this sense, a carefully chosen stone becomes both a style statement and a personal tool, harmonising aesthetic appeal with cosmic alignment. Jewellery, then, becomes a dialogue between the wearer and the universe. The next time you choose a piece, consider not just how it looks, but how it works for you. What appears to be a sparkling accessory could be an ally – attuned to your chart, your number and your intentions – a reminder that sometimes, the cosmos fits perfectly on your finger. article_title: How To Wear Big Shorts Without Looking Like Adam Sandler | Grazia India
sub_title: Big shorts are everywhere this summer. Here's how to style Bermudas, jorts and oversized shorts for every aesthetic without looking sloppy.
article_content: Your guide to styling the season's most comfortable trend. No disrespect to Adam Sandler, whose oversized basketball shorts and XXL tees have become a style category of their own. But while his famously laid-back uniform has inspired countless memes (and, let's be honest, a few fashion editorials), there's another way to wear the season's biggest shorts trend. With temperatures climbing and heatwaves becoming the new summer normal, comfort has officially become fashion's biggest priority. Unsurprisingly, big shorts have followed suit, popping up everywhere from runway collections to off-duty street style. Oversized, it turns out, doesn't have to mean underdressed. Whether you're reaching for jorts, tailored Bermudas or sporty silhouettes, it's less about the shorts themselves and more about the vibe you're creating. The trick is balance. So, the bigger the shorts, the more fitted or polished the rest of your outfit should be. If Your Style Is Quiet Luxury Big shorts don't have to read casual. A pair of tailored Bermuda shorts styled with a crisp button-down, a fitted tank, or a lightweight knit instantly feels elevated. Finish the look with loafers, ballet flats or sleek sandals, and keep accessories minimal. The result is understated, polished and quietly expensive-looking. A post shared by Mckenna Grace (@mckennagraceful) If You're Leaning Sporty Athletic shorts have officially graduated from the gym. Pair them with a fitted racerback tank, a vintage-inspired jersey or a rugby shirt, then add retro sneakers, crew socks and a baseball cap. It's an easy off-duty formula that feels sporty without looking like you're headed to a workout. A post shared by adidas Originals (@adidasoriginals) If You're the Cool Girl Oversized denim jorts have become the unofficial hero piece of cool-girl summer dressing. Style them with a baby tee, a ribbed tank or an oversized shirt left unbuttoned over a crop top. Finish with chunky sneakers or boots, slim sunglasses and a shoulder bag for that effortless street-style energy. A post shared by Mika! (@mika.abdalla) A post shared by Masoom Minawala Mehta (@masoomminawala) If You're On Vacation Mode Big shorts and warm-weather getaways go hand in hand. Swap tailored Bermudas for a breezy pair of culottes or wide-leg shorts, then style them with a fitted knit or a cropped top for that effortless, jet-set polish. Add strappy sandals, sleek sunglasses and a structured mini bag, and you've got a look that works just as well for hotel lobbies as it does for beach clubs. A post shared by Eva Longoria Baston (@evalongoria) If You're Taking Them to the Office Yes, big shorts can make it to the office. The key is to choose a tailored pair and style it with structured separates. A waistcoat, an oversized blazer or a tucked-in shirt instantly sharpens the silhouette, while loafers, slingbacks or low heels complete the polished look. A post shared by FCC Daily (@fccdaily) A post shared by Sofia Richie Grainge (@sofiagrainge) If You Actually Want the Adam Sandler Aesthetic Dressing like Adam Sandler isn't necessarily a fashion faux pas anymore. His signature combination of baggy basketball shorts, an oversized graphic tee, crew socks and chunky sneakers has quietly become its own aesthetic, embraced for its unapologetic comfort and carefree attitude. If that's the vibe you're after, commit to it. Once the look feels intentional, it stops looking accidental. A post shared by erl (@erl) Big shorts are one of those rare trends that are equal parts comfortable and stylish. Whether you're drawn to quiet luxury, sporty dressing, cool-girl street style or even full-blown Adam Sandler mode, the secret isn't the shorts, it's how you style them. Wear them with intention, and they'll do the rest. Disclaimer: This article offers general fashion and lifestyle inspiration. Individual results, preferences, and styling outcomes may vary.

article_title: South India's Madras Checks And Koodai Are Officially Cool Again | Grazia India
sub_title: The koodai and Madras checks are having a global glow-up as heritage, nostalgia and craftsmanship become fashion's biggest flex.
article_content: From local markets to luxury, South India's icons are cool again Growing up in South India, some things felt so ordinary that you almost stopped noticing them. The colourful plastic koodai swinging from someone's arm at the local market, stacks of them hanging outside tiny roadside shops, and Madras checks showing up everywhere, from lungis drying on balconies to grocery bags, kitchen towels and shirts worn by uncles bargaining over vegetables. Every bustling market had them. Every neighbourhood had them. They weren't 'design', they were simply everyday life. They carried groceries, flowers, lunch boxes and stories long before anyone thought to call them aesthetic. Fast-forward to now, and suddenly the same koodai and Madras checks are having a full-blown glow-up. They're popping up in beautifully curated homes, fashion editorials, designer collections and Instagram mood boards, proving that the coolest things were quietly sitting in our local markets all along. What once felt deeply familiar is now being rediscovered through a new lens, one that celebrates vernacular craft, regional identity and the beauty of objects with history. Maybe this isn't nostalgia at all.  It's a generation finally realising that home has always been the original luxury. That shift says a lot about where design is headed. After years of looking outward to Scandinavian minimalism, Japanese restraint or European heritage, people are beginning to look inward instead. Across fashion, interiors and lifestyle, there's a growing appetite for objects that carry memory, provenance and a sense of place. The new luxury isn't something anonymous or mass-produced – it's something with a story. And increasingly, those stories are beginning in local markets, artisan workshops and neighbourhood communities that have quietly preserved these traditions for decades. A post shared by The Manjapai Collective ™ (@manjapaicollective) Few objects embody that better than the humble koodai . Woven from colourful flat plastic wire, the basket has long been an indispensable part of daily life across Tamil Nadu, Kerala and Pondicherry. It's lightweight, waterproof, unbelievably sturdy and comes in endless combinations of checks, florals, geometric patterns and playful motifs. Long before 'functional fashion' became a Pinterest trend, the koodai was doing exactly that, moving effortlessly from vegetable markets to office commutes, temple visits and beach days without ever trying to be fashionable. A post shared by Malgudi | Home Decor (@malgudi.in) Today, a new generation of homegrown brands is helping the koodai find an entirely new audience. Labels like The Manjapai Collective, Koodai Kadaii, Malgudi, Filemot, Koodaikind, aren't trying to reinvent the basket but rather they're restoring the context around it. Their work is rooted in celebrating everyday vernacular objects that were often dismissed simply because they were everywhere. The Manjapai, named after Tamil Nadu's iconic yellow cloth bag, has built an entire design language around familiar cultural symbols, from kolam motifs to neighbourhood tea stalls while Koodai Kadaii works closely with artisans to preserve traditional weaving techniques and create sustainable livelihoods. Filemot meanwhile, is reintroducing regional craft into contemporary homes, proving that heritage belongs in everyday life rather than behind museum glass. A post shared by koodai kadaii (@koodaikadaii) The loodai's biggest flex, though, might be something luxury has spent decades trying to manufacture: Longevity. In a world obsessed with sustainability, these baskets have quietly been practising it all along. Yes, they're woven from plastic wire, but one koodai can easily outlive countless trendy handbags. It isn't designed for one season or one aesthetic. It simply becomes part of your life, carrying vegetables one day, a laptop the next, and beach towels over the weekend. It reminds us that sustainability isn't always about new materials, sometimes it's about making things that simply refuse to become obsolete. A post shared by Darwaza (@shop.darwaza) The comeback story of Madras checks is just as compelling. Long before the pattern found its way onto luxury runways or Pinterest mood boards, it belonged to South India's coastline. Woven from lightweight cotton in and around present-day Chennai, the colourful checked fabric was originally worn by fishing communities and workers who needed breathable clothing for the region's tropical climate. Handwoven on pit looms and coloured using vegetable dyes, every piece carried subtle irregularities that made it unmistakably handmade. Then came the East India Company, which transformed Madras into one of the world's biggest textile trading hubs, exporting the fabric across Europe and eventually the United States. By the 1950s, Madras checks had become a defining symbol of Ivy League dressing after American brands like Brooks Brothers embraced the textile for breezy summer shirts and tailored blazers. What many people knew simply as 'Madras' slowly evolved into an old-money wardrobe staple, even as its South Indian origins faded into the background. Today, that story is coming full circle, with designers reclaiming the textile through a distinctly Indian lens while simultaneously pushing it into exciting new territory. A post shared by No Grey Area (@nogreyarea_official) If you're wondering how Madras checks differs from every other checked fabric flooding your feed, here's the cheat sheet. Madras is woven from yarn-dyed cotton, giving it layered colours that soften beautifully over time. Gingham sticks to crisp two-tone symmetry, tartan is denser and rooted in Scottish heritage, while plaid is simply the umbrella category that encompasses multiple checked patterns. Madras, meanwhile, remains unmistakably light, breathable and deeply tied to Chennai's weaving history. Contemporary designers are proving just how versatile that heritage can be. The revival doesn't stop on the runway. Labels like No Grey Area, Ciceroni, The Jodi Life, Nicobar, Tree and Poetry, Kai by sobana, Hindostan Archive, Kartik Research, Imli Dana, Huemn and Ituvana are giving Madras checks fresh life through contemporary ready-to-wear. Think relaxed camp-collar shirts, handloom co-ords, wrap dresses, patchwork skirts, pre-stitched lungi skirts and oversized silhouettes that feel as relevant in Mumbai or Bengaluru as they do in New York or London. A post shared by ituvana (@ituvana) Perhaps no brand captures that global journey better than Original Madras Trading Company (OMTC). Based in New York but deeply rooted in Chennai, the label represents three generations of a family that helped introduce authentic Madras fabric to the American market decades ago. Today, OMTC continues that legacy by producing handwoven cotton shirts, hoodies, shorts, robes and veshtis in Chennai before sending them back out into the world. It's a beautiful full-circle moment, one where a textile that travelled across continents during colonial trade is now returning as a celebrated symbol of Indian craftsmanship rather than simply another export. A post shared by Original Madras Trading Co. (@originalmadrastradingco) Ultimately, the resurgence of the Koodai and Madras checks is about a generation choosing authenticity over algorithms. In a world where aesthetics can be bought with a click, these objects offer something rarer: Context. They remind us who made them, where they came from and why they mattered long before they became fashionable. Disclaimer: This article offers general fashion and lifestyle inspiration. article_title: The 2,000-Year-Old Muse Behind Indian Fashion's Current Debate | Grazia India
sub_title: Indian designers have long drawn inspiration from temple sculptures. But when the references overlap, where does homage end and repetition begin?
article_content: Indian designers, temple sculptures and the debate over originality. Indian fashion has always found itself looking backwards in order to move forwards. Long before archive accounts became the industry’s favourite research tools, designers were turning to India’s own monuments for inspiration. The voluptuous yakshis of the Mauryan period, the celestial apsaras dancing across Khajuraho’s sandstone walls, the sculptural grace of Chola bronzes and the elaborate jewellery adorning Gupta-era devis have shaped Indian couture for decades. These sculptures possess everything fashion continually seeks – sensuality, ornamentation, craftsmanship, mythology and an understanding of the body that feels at once timeless and surprisingly modern. It is hardly surprising, then, that they continue to resurface on the runway. Tarun Tahiliani explored the sensuality of Indian mythology and temple sculpture in his Spring/Summer 2001 collection, describing his work as an echo of “a legacy where fabric isn’t worn, it’s sculpted.” More than two decades later, Gaurav Gupta’s ‘Carved in Time’ revisited the sacred feminine through sculptural breastplates inspired by Mauryan yakshi figures and Gupta temple devis. Earlier this year, Central Saint Martins graduate Dhruv Bandil’s acclaimed collection ‘Awakening Kakanmath Kalavatis’ looked to the weathered sculptures of Madhya Pradesh’s Kakanmath Temple, painstakingly recreating centuries-old stone textures through hand stitching, experimental dyeing and textile manipulation. The muse, it seems, has never really changed. Rahul Mishra’s ‘Devi’, unveiled at Paris Haute Couture Week, became the latest interpretation of that enduring visual language. Inspired by India’s temple sculptures, the collection transformed carved stone into featherlight couture through intricate zardozi, dabka , crystals and bugle beads. Think: Sculptural breastplates, ceremonial crowns and jewelleryheavy silhouettes drew directly from the visual vocabulary of ancient Indian temples. The collection was immediately celebrated for showcasing Indian craftsmanship on one of fashion’s most prestigious stages. Celebrities including Cardi B and Isha Ambani attended the show wearing custom Rahul Mishra, while critics praised the technical brilliance of the embroidery and its deeply rooted narrative. But almost as quickly as applause came comparison. On the very day ‘Devi’ debuted in Paris, Gaurav Gupta shared images from ‘Carved in Time’, his own exploration of temple iconography and sculptural forms. Soon afterwards, Tarun Tahiliani revisited his Spring/Summer 2001 collection, reminding audiences that Indian mythology and temple sensuality had informed his work decades earlier. Social media built timelines, juxtaposed images and invited comparisons. Before long, the conversation had expanded far beyond Mishra’s collection. Indian temple sculpture is one of the richest visual archives in the country, revisited by painters, filmmakers, photographers, jewellers and fashion designers alike. The real question isn’t why multiple designers are inspired by the same source, but how each chooses to interpret it. Writer and journalist Praachi Raniwala believes the answer begins with acknowledging that cultural heritage can never belong to one individual. “I think my overall take on the situation was that no one brand, design house or designer can lay claim to culture, right? Or a particular part of history, a certain sculpture or a certain monument. I feel like they’re part of a larger cultural fabric which designers tap into from time to time for inspiration. The key is that it needs to be interpreted in their own ways,” explains Raniwala. Her perspective reflects a broader truth about fashion history, because very few designers create in complete isolation. Yves Saint Laurent looked to Mondrian, Alexander McQueen mined Victorian mourning rituals, and John Galliano referenced the Belle Époque. Originality has rarely meant inventing a completely new language; more often, it lies in speaking an old one differently. Raniwala also believes the controversy overshadowed a far more significant milestone: The growing presence of Indian designers on the global stage. “The focus ended up shifting from the fact that we’re wearing India on our sleeves while showing globally, as opposed to trying to pander to what the West expects from us” – Praachi Raniwala, fashion writer and journalist For years, Indian designers presenting internationally often found themselves boxed into familiar Western expectations of exoticism. Today, designers like Mishra, Gupta and others are instead presenting local references on their own terms. Temple architecture, regional craftsmanship and ancient philosophies are no longer being translated for Western audiences; they are being presented as contemporary luxury in their own right. “Designers collectively are trying to dispel this myth that we’re all about just maximalism or embroideries and colours, and make a statement that while our crafts and techniques may be ancient and carry a lot of heritage and weight, they’re just as relevant for these times and in every part of the world, not just for Indians,” says Raniwala. Fashion journalist and critic Shweta Shiware agrees that the debate should move beyond simply identifying references. “Fashion has always evolved through references, quotations and reinterpretation. Designers constantly look to art, history and each other’s work. The important question isn’t whether inspiration exists, but whether a designer transforms it into something recognisably their own. Originality often lies in interpretation rather than invention,” she explains. “Temple architecture continues to inspire fashion because it brings together craftsmanship, history, symbolism, human emotion and the body. What makes the work individual is the journey behind it, when the research began, how deeply it was explored, the techniques used and the visual language that came out of it” – Dhruv Bandil, fashion designer For designer Dhruv Bandil, whose own graduate collection centred around the partially damaged sculptures of Kakanmath Temple, shared that inspiration is not the issue. The distinction lies in what happens after the research begins. “Temple architecture continues to inspire fashion because it brings together craftsmanship, history, symbolism, human emotion and the body. What makes the work individual is the journey behind it, when the research began, how deeply it was explored, the techniques used and the visual language that came out of it,” he says. His own collection wasn’t simply about reproducing sculpture, but imagining the incomplete identities of damaged temple figures through clothing. Stone grey, soot black and terracotta eventually gave way to vivid pinks, oranges and blues, while cracked surfaces and eroded edges were painstakingly recreated through fabric manipulation and embroidery. For Bandil, that process of interpretation is what transforms history into design. Yet he also raises an important question about power within the fashion industry. “My concern is not with inspiration itself, but with what can happen when a young designer’s graduate work enters the public domain and begins to influence larger fashion conversations. Graduate collections are often created with very little money, support or protection, but they can still hold incredibly strong and original ideas. When those ideas begin appearing in wider industry spaces, I think it becomes important to speak about credit, acknowledgement and the power structures that shape whose work is seen and valued,” says Bandil. An industry once content to celebrate celebrity front rows and extraordinary craftsmanship is now debating research, references, representation and authorship with the seriousness usually reserved for art or cinema. That’s a sign of maturity. India’s temples have always been repositories of stories. Today, they remain one of fashion’s richest archives. Designers will continue to return to them, just as artists always have. When the inspiration is shared, originality isn’t about staking a claim – but about bringing a fresh perspective to a timeless source. article_title: AMRTA and FAVORI's New Mumbai Concept Store Is Redefining The Way We Shop | Grazia India
sub_title: AMRTA and FAVORI debut The Concept Store in Mumbai, blending inclusive fashion, handcrafted accessories and immersive retail under one thoughtfully designed roof.
article_content: Fashion, craftsmanship and immersive retail find a new home at Mumbai's latest concept store AMRTA, the art-inspired fashion label by Guneet Kondal, and FAVORI, the accessories brand co-founded by Kavita Bhatia and Rajiv Bhatia, are opening The Concept Store, a 700 sq. ft. space that feels nothing like a shop and everything like a world you want to step into. At its heart is a premise AMRTA has quietly built its name on that made-to-measure craftsmanship should fit everybody, not just the ones a size chart finds convenient. The pieces are available up to 6XL, with made-to-order and full customisation offered as standard silhouette, embroidery, fit, because fashion, Kondal believes, should adapt to the woman, not the other way around. The two founders first met in 2014 while working together at a renowned German fashion house, bonding over a shared obsession with craftsmanship, creativity and creating things people would genuinely cherish. What started as professional respect grew into a decade-long friendship and, eventually, a shared dream; a destination where every product was chosen because it carried a story. That conversation has finally become a reality. Designed around natural materials, warm textures and contemporary Indian aesthetics, the store is closer to a beautifully arranged home than anything you would call conventional retail. Nothing here is accidental. Every piece has been selected for its craftsmanship, its story and its ability to mean something long after it leaves the store. For Kondal, this moment has been a long time coming. She spent nearly two decades designing for global fashion houses before founding AMRTA, a label where every garment is conceived as a collectible work of art. The vision of a space where fashion and art could genuinely coexist, not just share a room, has been with her since childhood. It now has a postcode. For the Bhatias, The Concept Store is the natural next chapter for FAVORI, built on the conviction that a beautifully crafted bag deserves the same thoughtfulness as the outfit it accompanies. At the label, bags are designed with ease in mind, which integrate seamlessly into your everyday life, without the need to overthink. Versatile, functional, and quietly refined, they are made to be worn on repeat. Inside, AMRTA brings three worlds to the floor, each available in sizes up to 6XL with made-to-order customisation across silhouette, embroidery and fit. First, contemporary Indian occasion wear drawn from the rich visual language of Pichwai art, made for bridesmaids, soirees and every celebration worth remembering. Second, resort wear that is effortless and elegant, the kind that travels as well as it photographs. Third, Wild Poetry, a collection for everyday life that refuses to be forgettable, built around comfort, quiet confidence and the luxury of dressing entirely for yourself; in a fit that's actually yours. “ The launch of our first flagship store is a defining milestone for AMRTA. Since the beginning, we have envisioned it as more than a fashion label, it is a world shaped by craftsmanship, storytelling and timeless femininity, where every woman, in every size, can find a fit that is truly her own. In partnership with FAVORI, we have created a destination where fashion, accessories, art and design come together to reflect the life of the contemporary woman. We hope it becomes a place not just to shop, but to linger, to discover something new each time, and to fall in love with the details all over again,” shares Kondal. FAVORI arrives with equal intention. The Woven Theory is a study in handwoven craftsmanship and conscious material choices: Relaxed silhouettes and easy crossbodies that move with you through the day, priced to be within reach without compromising on quality. The Brunée Collection carries a more personal weight. Created to mark FAVORI's first boutique anniversary in India, it is warm in every sense with rich suedes, deep browns and textures that feel as considered as they look. Between the two, every side of FAVORI's design language finds its voice. “This store is not just about what we sell, but how it makes you feel when you walk in – comfortable, inspired, and at ease," shares Kavita Bhatia. The store itself is designed to be experienced. Conceived as a gallery-like environment, it asks you to slow down and notice things. Every six weeks, that experience deepens further through curated activations, founder conversations, exclusive previews, styling sessions and pop-up collaborations that ensure no two visits feel quite the same.
